region.name: Fintech Engineering Leadership Playbook
region.summary: Engineering leadership guidance for a growing fintech covering interview scorecards, tech lead and code review expectations, meeting hygiene, Q4 priorities and SOC 2 readiness, 18-month goals, and Series B deck and technical diligence preparation.

brief.text:
This region is the engineering leadership playbook for Stencil, a money-movement fintech scaling its engineering team from 14 to 25 engineers after closing a Series B. It codifies working norms for code review, hiring, meetings, and technical decisions. Architecture changes require an ADR, two reviewers including the affected pod's tech lead, and discussion in #eng-architecture. Reviewers are expected to read the whole diff, ask "what's the failure mode?" for every non-trivial change (an open risk item at severity 70), and give clear feedback. Authors write meaningful PR descriptions, self-review before requesting review, and engage with feedback. Tech leads own their pod's architecture, dependencies, and tech debt, write at least 40% code, act as bar-raiser on risky reviews, negotiate sprint scope, and send weekly updates. Engineers may use AI tools like Claude and Cursor but personally own all code that lands in main. Culture guidance also asks people to read the room by noticing teammates' state.

Hiring and meeting hygiene are concrete. Backend interview scorecards cover communication, ownership, and an optional fintech/money-domain awareness dimension. The communication dimension asks how well a candidate explains their thinking, listens, and pushes back. The domain dimension checks whether they understand idempotency and why a retry must never move money twice (an open todo at severity 73). Meeting norms say to leave any meeting where you neither contribute nor learn. The tech-product sync, the hiring sync, and the weekly security review were cancelled or consolidated. All-hands, TL 1:1s, and the founder-CTO weekly are protected. Any new recurring meeting must be justified with a doc. New engineers are coached to minimize meeting overhead and default to async.

The region also covers Q4 planning and fundraising. Q4 priorities #4 and #5 are SOC 2 Type II readiness and hiring. Open SOC 2 gaps include the Q3 access review (owner Sam Whitfield, severity 27), getting MDM to 100% (severity 17), and vendor risk assessment. The hiring priority covers a VP Engineering decision and the first post-close hiring wave. Explicit Q4 non-goals are a card issuing build, Postgres sharding, growth experiments on money flows, and new Go services. For the Series B deck, the draft 'How we built it' slide presents a three-layer architecture: mobile, backend services, and a separate money movement layer. Its talking points are Postgres as system of record and compliance treated as engineering. The slides deliberately leave out tech stack details, headcount, vendor names, and code metrics. Narrative ownership is split with Aleks, and a technical diligence room checklist must be prepared before the deck is sent. Typical questions this region answers include who must review an architecture PR, what tech leads are accountable for, what is out of scope in Q4, what SOC 2 items remain open, how to score a backend candidate, and what to include or exclude in Series B materials.

items.title: Decision: Cancel low-value recurring meetings
items.summary: Cross-functional tech-product sync cancelled, hiring sync folded into TL sync, weekly security review replaced by async Slack thread plus monthly meeting.

items.title: Decision: Card issuing soft launch moved to Q1 2027
items.summary: Q4 limited to design and vendor setup; Postgres sharding, new Go services outside money movement, and growth experiments on money flows until GA plus two weeks are also out of scope.
